#### Weighting to Improve Fit {#sec-pmd-634}

[**Weighting**]{#sec-pmd-634-weighting}

Another approach when the assumption of constant variance of the errors is violated is to perform a [weighted fit](#sec-pmd-143). In a weighted fit, we give less weight to the less precise measurements and more weight to more precise measurements when estimating the unknown parameters in the model.

[**Finding an Appropriate Weight Function**]{#sec-pmd-634-weight-function}

Techniques for determining an appropriate weight function were discussed in detail in [Section 4.4.5.2](#sec-pmd-452). In this case, we have replication in the data, so we can fit the power model

$$\ln(\hat\sigma_i^2) = \ln(\gamma_1 x_i^{\gamma_2}) = \ln(\gamma_1) + \gamma_2 \ln(x_i)$$

to the variances from each set of replicates in the data and use

$$w_i = \frac{1}{x_i^{\hat\gamma_2}}$$

for the weights.

[**Fit for Estimating Weights**]{#sec-pmd-634-weight-fit}

The following results were obtained for the fit of ln(variances) against ln(means) for the replicate groups.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
chwirut <- read_table(
  here::here("datasets", "CHWIRUT1.DAT"),
  skip = 25,
  col_names = c("response", "metal_distance")
)

replicate_groups <- chwirut |>
  group_by(metal_distance) |>
  summarise(var_response = var(response))

weight_fit <- lm(log(var_response) ~ log(metal_distance), data = replicate_groups)
summary(weight_fit)
```

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pmd-634-weight-function
#| fig-cap: "ln(Replicate variances) versus ln(metal distance), with the fitted power-function model"
replicate_groups <- replicate_groups |> mutate(residual_weight = resid(weight_fit))

ggplot(replicate_groups, aes(log(metal_distance), log(var_response))) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "ln(Metal Distance)", y = "ln(Replicate Variances)") +
  theme_light()
```

The fit output and plot from the replicate variances against the replicate means shows that the linear fit provides a reasonable fit, with an estimated slope of -1.1128.

Based on this fit, we used an estimate of -1.0 for the exponent in the weighting function, so the weight for each observation is

$$w_i = \frac{1}{x_i^{-1}} = x_i$$

[**Residual Plot for Weight Function**]{#sec-pmd-634-weight-residuals}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pmd-634-weight-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Residuals from the fit for estimating the weight function"
ggplot(replicate_groups, aes(log(metal_distance), residual_weight)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "ln(Metal Distance)", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_light()
```

The residual plot from the fit to determine an appropriate weighting function reveals no obvious problems.

[**Numerical Results from Weighted Fit**]{#sec-pmd-634-weighted-fit}

The results of the weighted fit are shown below.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
chwirut <- chwirut |> mutate(w = metal_distance)

outw <- nls(
  response ~ exp(-b1 * metal_distance) / (b2 + b3 * metal_distance),
  data = chwirut,
  start = list(b1 = 0.1, b2 = 0.1, b3 = 0.1),
  weights = w
)

summary(outw)
```

::: {.callout-note}
NIST's own reference R script for this case study fits the weighted model using a manually constructed zero-formula weighted least squares call, `nls(~ sqrt(w) * (resp - exp(-b1*dist)/(b2 + b3*dist)), start = list(...))`, rather than R's `weights =` argument to `nls()`. The two approaches produce identical parameter estimates and standard errors, so this book uses the simpler `weights =` form shown above.
:::

[**Plot of Predicted Values**]{#sec-pmd-634-predicted}

To assess the quality of the weighted fit, we first generate a plot of the predicted line with the original data.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pmd-634-overlay
#| fig-cap: "Ultrasonic reference block data overlaid with the weighted fit"
chwirut <- chwirut |> mutate(fitted_w = fitted(outw), residuals_w = response - fitted_w)

ggplot(chwirut, aes(metal_distance, response)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted_w), color = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "Metal Distance", y = "Ultrasonic Response") +
  theme_light()
```

The plot of the predicted values with the data indicates a good fit. The model for the weighted fit is

$$\hat y = \frac{e^{-0.147 x}}{0.00528 + 0.0124 x}$$

[**6-Plot of Fit**]{#sec-pmd-634-6plot}

We need to verify that the weighted fit does not violate the regression assumptions. The 6-plot indicates that the regression assumptions are satisfied.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-pmd-634-6plot
#| fig-cap: "6-plot for the weighted fit, using weighted residuals"
chwirut <- chwirut |> mutate(weighted_residuals = sqrt(w) * residuals_w)

six_plot <- function(x, y, residual, fitted) {
  d <- tibble(x = x, y = y, residual = residual, fitted = fitted) |>
    mutate(lag_residual = lag(residual))

  p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
    geom_line(aes(y = fitted), color = "firebrick") +
    labs(x = "Metal Distance", y = "Ultrasonic Response", title = "Data with Fit") +
    theme_light()

  p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(x, residual)) +
    geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
    labs(x = "Metal Distance", y = "Weighted Residual", title = "Residuals vs Metal Distance") +
    theme_light()

  p3 <- ggplot(d, aes(fitted, residual)) +
    geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
    labs(x = "Predicted", y = "Weighted Residual", title = "Residuals vs Predicted") +
    theme_light()

  p4 <- ggplot(d, aes(lag_residual, residual)) +
    geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
    labs(x = "Residual[i-1]", y = "Residual[i]", title = "Lag Plot") +
    theme_light()

  p5 <- ggplot(d, aes(residual)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.6, color = "white") +
    labs(x = "Weighted Residual", y = "Count", title = "Histogram") +
    theme_light()

  p6 <- ggplot(d, aes(sample = residual)) +
    stat_qq(color = "steelblue") +
    stat_qq_line(color = "firebrick") +
    labs(x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Weighted Residual", title = "Normal Probability Plot") +
    theme_light()

  (p1 + p2 + p3) / (p4 + p5 + p6)
}

six_plot(chwirut$metal_distance, chwirut$response, chwirut$weighted_residuals, chwirut$fitted_w)
```

[**Plot of Residuals**]{#sec-pmd-634-residuals}

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
#| label: fig-pmd-634-residuals
#| fig-cap: "Weighted residuals from the weighted fit versus metal distance"
ggplot(chwirut, aes(metal_distance, weighted_residuals)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Metal Distance", y = "Weighted Residuals") +
  theme_light()
```

In order to check the assumption of equal error variances in more detail, we generate a full-sized version of the residuals versus the predictor variable. This plot suggests that the residuals now have approximately equal variability.
